newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Stage set for worse Israel-Palestinian relations.
newsitem.headline: Stage set for worse Israel-Palestinian relations.

text.p: Worsening relations between Israel and the Palestinians suffered yet another blow with the first fatality in 10 days of Palestinian unrest over Jewish settlement building in Arab East Jerusalem.
Palestinian hospital officials said Israeli troops shot Abdullah Khalil Abdullah, 20, dead during clashes on the outskirts of the Palestinian self-rule enclave of Ramallah.

Thousands of Israeli police and troops, backed by tanks and helicopters, were already on alert against civil violence peaking on Sunday, the annual "Land Day" when Israeli Arabs stage protests against government confiscations of land.
Abdullah's death suggested that clashes were even more likely on the day when Christian pilgrims flock to sites sacred to them in the Holy Land for Easter celebrations.
"This killing is a declaration of war," said Palestinian Authority Finance Minister Mohammed Nashashibi.

An honour guard of red-bereted Palestinian security forces escorted Abdullah's body to his village of Beit Sahour late on Saturday and chanted: "Your blood was not spilled in vain and we will take our revenge."
He is to be buried on Sunday at Beit Sahour beside Jabal Abu Ghneim, known as Har Homa in Hebrew, where Israel has started work on building its latest controversial Jewish settlement.
Hospital officials said 24 Palestinians were wounded by Israeli rubber bullets on Saturday and two were wounded by live ammunition.
The army said an initial investigation showed troops did not use live ammunition at Ramallah though they did in clashes with Palestinans at nearby Qalandya refugee camp.

Prospects for progress in Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations, already jeopardised by a row over the new settlement, were further damaged when an Islamist suicide bomber killed three Israelis last week.
The Palestinian Authority after a cabinet meeting issued a pleas to the United States and Europe to save the peace process, launched with such hope at Madrid in 1991.

It said: "The Palestinian leadership...calls on President Bill Clinton to save the peace process from possible collapse...(It) calls on the European states to continue their initiative and movement to save the peace process from collapsing."

The Authority earlier rejected Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's conditions for resuming peace talks. It denies his charge that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has given tacit approval for militants to lauch attacks.
Netanyahu, after meeting U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross on Friday, said Arafat must arrest militants, dismantle guerrilla groups and tighten security cooperation.
Palestinians say work on building the new settlement must be halted as it preempts the results of negotiations yet to be held in final peace talks on Jerusalem's status.

The Israeli Foreign Ministry described as an obstacle to peace a call by a committee headed by Morocco's King Hassan urging Arab and Moslem states to reconsider ties with Israel because of the new settlement.

But Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak predicted incessant violence until Israel stopped building settlements in East Jerusalem. He said Netanyahu had to abandon what he called a patronising attitude towards his Arab neighbours.
